signals.headline: A Number System No Model Can Read
signals.one_liner: Bangladeshi land titles record area in a base-16 positional fraction with its own Unicode glyphs; six multimodal LLMs return zero correct answers on 39% of question categories, and on arithmetic every model that emits a number loses to a constant-mean guess
signals.why_you: You are about to spend three years reading benchmark scores. This is the paper to keep beside them: it shows a capability can be entirely absent while the average still looks reassuringly non-zero.
signals.title: KhatianDoc: A Human-Verified Benchmark Diagnosing Multimodal LLM Failure on Bengali Legal Land Records
signals.summary: Land ownership in Bangladesh is recorded in RS Khatians, whose area fields use Ana-Ganda-Kora-Kranti-Til, a base-16 positional fraction system with dedicated Unicode glyphs, no mainstream font, and no coverage in any OCR pipeline or tokenizer. The authors built a four-task benchmark from 107 real records from the Munshiganj land office: symbol recognition, base-16-to-decimal conversion, structured field extraction, and legal question answering over 1,634 QA pairs. Ground truth was transcribed by hand and verified to full agreement by a land-law practitioner, then anonymised through positional tokens that preserve the referential distinctions multi-hop questions depend on. Six multimodal LLMs from 8B to 72B+ were evaluated under a fixed zero-shot protocol. Five QA categories, 39.3% of the stratified set, returned zero correct answers from every model. On the arithmetic task, every model that emitted a number scored below a constant-mean baseline, with exact- and near-match scores coinciding: decorrelation, not approximation. The authors also audit their own metrics, correcting a refusal-scoring bug and flagging one inflated metadata figure as an upper bound.
signals.why_it_matters: The paper is explicit that this is not a performance gap but the absence of a capability. That distinction is normally invisible, because a benchmark reports one number averaged across categories where the model has some competence and categories where it has none. The constant-mean baseline is the instrument that makes the difference legible: if predicting the average beats your model, the model is not doing the task weakly, it is not doing it at all.
signals.why_you_should_care: Two habits fall out and both are cheap. First, never read a benchmark average without asking what the floor is: a constant, a majority class, a random draw. Second, notice where this failure lives. Not in the model's reasoning but in the tokenizer and the font pipeline. The record was machine-readable in principle and unreachable in practice because nobody built the glyphs. That is a cultural-data problem wearing an AI costume, and it is exactly the kind your intersection is supposed to be good at noticing.
signals.suggested_action: Take one task you currently trust a model with — translating a Chinese source, pulling a table out of a PDF, summarising a paper you haven't read — and write the dumbest possible baseline for it. Constant, majority label, first row. Run both twenty times on cases you can verify yourself. If the baseline wins, you have not found a weak model; you have found a missing capability, and those need different fixes.

signals.headline: An Agent Can Keep Its Memory and Still Forget
signals.one_liner: Hold the memory store fixed and swap the model: fixed-schema knowledge graphs shift by 0.0004, model-written notes swing +9.91 or −13.28 points, and repair without the raw source fails in all 48 cases
signals.why_you: Phase 9 of your coach is, in this paper's vocabulary, a compressed-notes store with a schema bolted on. The paper tells you which half survives your next model upgrade and which half doesn't — before you finish building it.
signals.title: Does Your Agent's Memory Survive a Model Upgrade? A Controlled Study of Memory Portability
signals.summary: The authors take 48 synthetic agent histories with randomised answer codes and preserve the same history in four formats: verbatim long-context reading, chunked retrieval-augmented generation, model-compressed natural-language notes, and a fixed-schema knowledge graph. They then swap the writer or reader model and measure what survives. Fixed-schema graphs transfer almost perfectly, with accuracy changing by +0.0004 ± 0.0020 after a writer swap. Compressed notes are strongly model-coupled, shifting asymmetrically by +9.91 or −13.28 percentage points depending on migration direction, so A→B tells you nothing about B→A. In RAG, a 50/50 mixed embedding index recovers only 4.96 points of the 11.90-point gain available from full re-embedding — mixing vector spaces is close to worst-of-both. Diagnostic decomposition attributes 80% of the notes deficit to information lost during initial compression, and 81% of the RAG deficit to retrieval failure: the two formats break in different places. Finally, store-only repair of compressed notes fails to reach a 90% recovery target in all 48 cases, while retaining the raw source history enables recovery in 34 of 48 for one tested direction.
signals.why_it_matters: It reframes agent memory from a feature into a lifecycle object with a migration cost. The failure is silent — no error, no crash, the store still returns results, accuracy simply drops — which makes it the kind of bug that survives a demo and dies after deployment. It also reframes compression: summarising is not free storage, it is lossy encoding whose cost is deferred to whoever upgrades the model next.
signals.why_you_should_care: Your Phase 9 spec already insists on Evidence ID, reasoning and confidence on every suggestion, and on a rule-engine fallback. This paper is the argument for a fourth requirement you have not written down: keep the raw turn history even after the structured summary exists. The summary is what gets read; the raw history is what lets you rebuild when the model changes. Store-only repair failing 48 times out of 48 is the entire case in one number.
signals.suggested_action: Open your Phase 9 spec and add one line under persistence: raw conversation history is append-only and is never deleted by a compression step, even when the structured record is complete. Then mark which of your coach's fields are fixed-schema and which are free text. The paper says only the first kind is portable.

signals.headline: Agents Building Agents: 23.9% Against an Expert's 82.2%
signals.one_liner: Hand a coding agent the records, a client with requirements and a production API, and ask it to deliver a working service agent — the strongest configuration passes under a quarter of held-out user simulations, and the failure is one any junior consultant would recognise
signals.why_you: The three failure modes the paper names — shallow queries instead of reading the records, almost no communication with the client, shipping the first design that runs — are the same three you would be tempted by. It is a mirror held up to how you build, not only to what models can do.
signals.title: τ^τ-Bench: An Environment for End-To-End, Realistic Agent Construction
signals.summary: Rather than scoring an agent on a fixed task, this benchmark makes building the agent the task. A developer agent receives what a real client engagement provides: the records a business actually keeps, a client holding requirements, a production API that operations must run through, a codebase to inherit, and limits on serving cost and model choice. From that it must deliver a complete customer-service agent, scored by deploying that agent against held-out simulated users. Across 53 tasks spanning four domains, the strongest configuration, Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code, passes 23.9% of evaluation simulations, against an expert-authored reference ceiling of 82.2%. The authors characterise the failures as ones human agent developers also see: models issue shallow queries in place of deep comprehension of the records, communicate almost nothing to the client, and experiment too little with agent architecture and serving spend, shipping the first design that runs.
signals.why_it_matters: Most agent benchmarks measure whether a model can complete a task inside a harness someone else built. This one measures whether it can do the engagement, which is where the difficulty actually lives once models are strong. The 58-point gap between the best system and an expert is a rarer and more honest number than another leaderboard delta.
signals.why_you_should_care: You are building a system in which an LLM sits behind a structured interface and is asked to produce advice for one specific person. That is an engagement, not a task. The diagnosis transfers almost word for word: do not query your context store shallowly, do not assume you know what the user wanted without asking, and do not ship the first prompt that returns valid JSON.
signals.suggested_action: Take the last thing you built with an LLM in the loop and write down the three questions you never asked: what the data actually contained, what the user actually wanted, and what a second architecture would have cost. If you cannot answer all three from your own notes, you shipped the first design that ran.

signals.headline: The Model Doesn't Know What Machine It's Running On
signals.one_liner: State a memory and time budget in the prompt and the generated code changes shape by itself — bounded blocking, float32, memory-mapped buffers; at a 96 MB contract, correct-and-within-budget goes from 0/5 to 4/5
signals.why_you: It gives a name to something you have probably already felt: a plan that is technically right and institutionally impossible. The name is substrate blindness, and once you have it you will see it everywhere in cultural-sector work.
signals.title: Substrate-Aware AI Agents: Execution Context as a First-Class Input
signals.summary: The paper names a failure it calls substrate blindness: agents select actions in environments whose memory, execution-time, runtime, compute and operational constraints determine what counts as a suitable plan, yet those constraints are absent from the agent's planning state. It tests the proposition on numerical code generation, where implementation choices and their operational consequences are directly observable. Three frontier configurations generate code for a high-dimensional pairwise Euclidean-distance task either from the task alone or with a 128 MB RAM and 10.0 s wall-time contract. Contract disclosure reduced measured peak process memory in 13 of 14 executable index-aligned comparisons and reduced mean wall time in all three cohorts, making execution up to 3.1x faster. The changes were structural rather than cosmetic: bounded blocking, float32 retention, upper-triangle traversal, and in-place or memory-mapped buffers. At a tighter 96 MB contract, independently sampled contract-disclosed cohorts achieved correct-and-within-budget outcomes of 4/5, 5/5 and 3/5, against task-only outcomes of 0/5, 1/5 and 0/5.
signals.why_it_matters: The interesting claim is not that constraints help, which is obvious. It is that the constraint had to be stated in order to exist at all. Nothing about a distance-matrix task tells a model it will run on a laptop with 8 GB free, so it writes the version that assumes infinite memory, and that version is correct and unusable. Constraints are not limits on a plan; they are inputs to it, and withholding them is a reliable way to get the wrong answer.
signals.why_you_should_care: This generalises past code and it is the most transferable idea on today's radar. A museum with two servers, a course with a three-week deadline, your own MacBook on a train: each is a substrate, and a plan that ignores it is substrate-blind. You will be asked to propose computational work to people in cultural institutions. Knowing to ask what this actually has to run on, and who maintains it, before proposing anything is the difference between a plan and a proposal.
signals.suggested_action: For one week, add one line to every prompt where you ask a model for code or a plan: the machine, the memory ceiling, the time budget, and who has to maintain the result. Compare what comes back against what you used to get. That difference is the size of your own substrate blindness.

signals.headline: Knowledge as Mental Programs, Not Sentences
signals.one_liner: A model that represents hypotheses as programs mixing natural language with source code reproduces human anchoring and garden-pathing effects that both pure LLMs and classic Bayesian models miss
signals.why_you: It is the rare cognitive-science paper whose claim you can test on yourself in an afternoon, and it hands you a vocabulary — hypothesis space, program-like representation, approximate Bayesian update — for something you already do when you debug.
signals.title: Induction and Inquiry via Probabilistic Reasoning over Language and Code
signals.summary: The authors ask how humans grow and maintain abstract knowledge from the sparse, streaming, noisy data of experience, and argue that any computational account must satisfy three desiderata: it must be data- and compute-efficient, it must capture gradations of uncertainty to support intelligent inquiry and information gathering, and it must be flexible enough to represent the endless range of concepts people can learn. Their model encodes symbolic knowledge as mental programs that combine natural language with source code, and infers those programs sequentially using LLM-guided Bayesian learning algorithms. Across a range of behavioural studies it reproduces quantitative signatures of human inductive learning and active inquiry, including anchoring, garden-pathing and related effects. Pure LLMs and classic Bayesian models either fail at the underlying task, fail to reproduce human behaviour, or succeed only at exorbitant computational cost. The reading offered is that humans hold many hypotheses spanning language-like and program-like representations, revise them to approximate Bayesian updates, and use a bottom-up neural mechanism to keep inference tractable.
signals.why_it_matters: The hybrid is the point. Language alone is too vague to execute; code alone is too rigid to cover what people actually think about. Putting both in one representation, letting a neural system propose updates while a probabilistic framework scores them, produces human-like behaviour from components that are not individually human-like. It is also one of the few live answers to the question of what a concept is, computationally.
signals.why_you_should_care: Two things. Bayesian thinking is on your curiosity list marked not-started; this is a paper where Bayes does visible work inside a model of learning rather than sitting in a textbook chapter. Second, and more useful tomorrow: when you are stuck debugging you are already running this loop. You hold several hypotheses about the bug, each a mix of a vague story and a concrete mental program, and each test updates them. Knowing that is a formal process makes it much easier to notice when you have stopped updating and started defending one hypothesis.
signals.suggested_action: Next time you are stuck on a bug for more than twenty minutes, stop and write out every hypothesis you are currently holding, one line each. If you can only write one, that is the garden path — go find a second before you test anything.

signals.headline: Reading a Temple the Way You'd Read a Sentence
signals.one_liner: A $225,000 NEH grant puts an architectural historian and an NLP researcher on 180,000 excavated artefacts from the Athenian Agora, asking a model to induce the shape grammar of classical buildings instead of hand-coding it
signals.why_you: It is the closest thing to a worked example of your own trajectory: an art-trained person and a technical person splitting the difference, on Mediterranean material, with a real funding line behind it and a named archive you could visit.
signals.title: New AI Models Could Create More Accurate Visualizations of Classical Architecture
signals.summary: Kartik Goyal of the School of Interactive Computing and Myrsini Mamoli, an architectural historian jointly in the School of Architecture and the School of History and Sociology, received a $225,000 National Endowment for the Humanities grant to build models that help reconstruct classical Greek structures. Mamoli works at the Ancient Agora in Athens, where more than 180,000 artefacts have been uncovered and every discovery since 1933 has a digitised record. Her earlier work computed shape grammars — rule-based recursive visual systems, one per architectural style — by hand, in order to generate 2D reconstructions. The collaboration asks whether a model can discover those rules from the data at scale and then apply them recursively to propose reconstructions. Goyal has used comparable methods to trace the printing origins of early modern English books. Both are explicit about the risk: Goyal notes that running such models blindly risks incorporating undetected bias, and Mamoli frames AI as assisting scholarly work rather than replacing it.
signals.why_it_matters: The substantive move is inverting who writes the grammar. A shape grammar is normally authored by a scholar, which means it carries that scholar's assumptions about which features matter. Asking a model to induce the grammar from 180,000 records makes the assumptions visible and arguable: you can inspect the rules it found and disagree with them, which you cannot do with a person's intuition.
signals.why_you_should_care: Three reasons this lands on you specifically. It has the same shape as the Venice problem — a city with overwhelming archival density and nowhere near enough people to read it. It is a template for the interdisciplinary pairing you keep describing, where the historian holds the question and the ML person holds the method and neither defers. And note the funder: NEH, not NSF. Digital humanities money in this area comes from humanities councils, which means the proposal has to be legible as a humanities question first. Worth knowing well before you write one.
signals.suggested_action: Read the piece once for the method and once for the shape of the collaboration. Then write down, in two sentences, what the Venetian equivalent of the Agora record set is: which archive, which 180,000 items, which question nobody has the staff to ask. If you cannot name the archive, that is the actual first step.

signals.headline: A Ministry Ships Cultural Data With the Connector Attached
signals.one_liner: Korea's culture ministry will release five AI-ready cultural datasets — traditional music, policy QA, tourism, 3D heritage assets and patterns — and for the first time publish MCP linkage alongside them, so models connect rather than humans download
signals.why_you: It is a small administrative decision that quietly changes what open cultural data means, and you are building things that consume exactly this kind of interface while living in a city made of the stuff.
signals.title: Culture Ministry to Release Five Types of AI and High-value Public Data in the Cultural Sector for the First Time
signals.summary: On 3 September Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism announced it will open five high-value cultural datasets by December as national key data: traditional Korean music audio and images with expert annotation on genre, instrument, rhythm and expressive technique, from the National Gugak Center; policy QA datasets built from domestic and international government documents, from the National Library of Sejong; multilingual nationwide tourism information and regional video content, from the Korea Tourism Organization; and 3D cultural assets, Korean attire and traditional pattern data in AI-optimised formats, from the Korea Cultural Information Service. The last of these adds expert review of cultural and historical reliability and structures relationships between resources as an ontology. Five further datasets follow in 2026 and seven in 2027. The operationally new part is the delivery: the release will ship Model Context Protocol linkage information alongside the data, the ministry's first use of MCP, explicitly intended to move the system from public data people have to find and use toward cultural data easily connected and utilised by AI.
signals.why_it_matters: Two details are the actual news. First, the ontology layer: relationships and semantic information between cultural resources are modelled explicitly, so a system can learn that a pattern belongs to a period and a garment to a class rather than inferring it from filenames. Second, the MCP linkage: the unit of release stops being a file and becomes an addressable tool. That is a different theory of what open means for cultural data, and if it works it will be copied.
signals.why_you_should_care: You already live inside MCP-based tooling and you are about to spend several years in a city whose entire economy is cultural data. Watching a national ministry decide that the correct release format is a connector rather than a ZIP file is the early signal for how European institutions will do it — the Commission's common European data space for cultural heritage is aiming at tens of millions of licensed digital objects available for AI training by 2030. Whoever builds the interface layer for that, in either language, is doing work you would want to be able to do.
signals.suggested_action: Don't write about this, wire something. Find the smallest cultural dataset you can with a public API and expose three tools over MCP: search by period, fetch one record, list related records. Twenty minutes of plumbing, and you will have felt the difference between data you download and data you query.

pattern.label: PATTERN EMERGING
pattern.statement: Today's signals keep arriving at the same shape from different directions: the thing that looks like the system working is not the thing that is working. A land-record benchmark finds six multimodal models returning zero correct answers across nearly forty per cent of question categories, and the only instrument that reveals it is a baseline too stupid to be wrong — guess the average. A memory study finds an agent can keep its entire store and lose thirteen points of accuracy with no error raised, because the loss happened invisibly during compression. A construction benchmark finds the best system passing a quarter of what an expert passes, failing not at the task but at the engagement: too shallow with the records, too quiet with the client, too quick to ship. A code-generation paper finds that simply telling the model how much memory it has makes it write a different program, which means the constraint was always there and had simply been left out of the planning state. Four fields, one structure: performance is being produced by something other than capability. Which means the useful question is never how good is it, but what is it standing on, and what happens when that moves.

open_question.label: A QUESTION WORTH CARRYING
open_question.text: If a model's score can stay high while the capability underneath is absent, then what exactly are you measuring when you compare two systems — and how long do you want to keep calling that evaluation?

world.headline: A Number System No Model Can Read
world.sub: KhatianDoc builds 1,634 human-verified questions over real Bangladeshi land titles: six multimodal LLMs score zero on 39.3% of categories, and on arithmetic every model that answers loses to guessing the average
world.why: It separates a weak capability from an absent one, and shows the only instrument that can tell them apart is a baseline nobody would bother to submit

world.headline: An Agent Can Keep Its Memory and Still Forget
world.sub: Across 48 histories and four storage formats, fixed-schema graphs shift by 0.0004 after a model swap while compressed notes swing up to 13 points — and repair without the raw source fails every single time
world.why: It makes compression a deferred cost rather than free storage, and it names the exact line your own coach's persistence layer needs

world.headline: Reading a Temple Like a Sentence
world.sub: A $225,000 NEH grant has an architectural historian and an NLP researcher inducing the shape grammar of classical buildings from 180,000 excavated Agora records, instead of hand-authoring the rules
world.why: Inverting who writes the grammar turns a scholar's invisible assumptions into something you can inspect and argue with

think.question: Can a plan be correct and still be impossible?
think.explain: Yes, routinely. An agent asked to compute a large distance matrix with no memory or time budget writes the version that assumes infinite memory: correct, and it will not run. Disclosing a 128 MB and 10 second contract changed the generated code structurally — bounded blocking, float32, memory-mapped buffers — and moved correct-and-within-budget from 0/5 to 4/5 at a tighter 96 MB. The constraint was never a limit on the plan; it was an input to it.
think.why: It generalises past code. A museum with two servers, a three-week deadline, a laptop on a train: every one is a substrate, and a proposal that ignores the substrate is a proposal that will not survive contact with it.

think.question: How do you tell a weak capability from an absent one?
think.explain: You run a control that cannot be right for the right reasons: always predict the mean, always predict the most frequent label, always return the first row. In KhatianDoc's arithmetic task, every model that emitted a number scored below the constant-mean baseline, and exact- and near-match scores coincided — the outputs were decorrelated from the answer, not approximately correct. That coincidence is the signature of absence rather than weakness.
think.why: Because averages hide it. A benchmark reports one number across categories where the model has some competence and categories where it has none, and the zero categories are invisible in the total. A baseline you would be embarrassed to submit is the cheapest instrument that makes them visible.

look.subject: Ninety Years of Dirt, Digitised
look_for: That the excavation has run continuously since 1933 — this is a dataset accumulated by an institution, not by a project, which is precisely why it is dense enough to induce rules from
How little survives vertically: foundations and column drums. Every reconstruction anyone argues about is built on this much physical evidence
What the photograph leaves out — 180,000 catalogued artefacts exist somewhere off-frame, and that catalogue, not the ruins, is what the models actually read

discover.name: Melanie Mitchell
roles: Author, Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans
discover.desc: A computer scientist who took her PhD under Douglas Hofstadter and John Holland, and whose career has run through genetic algorithms, cellular automata, complex systems and analogical reasoning. For the past several years she has been doing something less fashionable than building models: insisting on the difference between a system that performs a task and a system that understands one. Her current work is on abstraction and analogy as the unsolved core of machine intelligence, and on how easily benchmark numbers conceal the absence of the thing they appear to measure.
discover.why: She has been making today's argument longer than anyone. KhatianDoc's distinction between a performance gap and the absence of a capability is, in her vocabulary, the difference between pattern matching and abstraction — and she has argued for years that the field keeps mistaking one for the other because the benchmarks reward it. She is also a working model of a career built precisely at the seam between cognitive science and AI, which is the seam you are trying to stand on.

explore.question: What is the dumbest possible baseline for the thing you most trust a model to do — and have you ever actually run it?
explore.start_name: KhatianDoc — the benchmark that used a constant-mean guess as a control

trail.title: Pick one task you would defend a model on
trail.hint: Translation, table extraction, summarising a paper you have not read. One task, not a benchmark suite — you need to be able to check the answers yourself.

trail.title: Write the baseline you would be embarrassed to submit
trail.hint: Always predict the mean. Always predict the most frequent label. Always return the first row. Ten lines, no intelligence in them at all.

trail.title: Run both on twenty cases you can verify
trail.hint: Score per category, never overall. The average is exactly where absence hides, and a single number will tell you nothing.

trail.title: Find the category where the baseline wins
trail.hint: In KhatianDoc there were five. When you find yours, you have located a missing capability — and no amount of better prompting will fix a missing capability.

explore.why: It takes an afternoon and permanently changes how you read an evaluation number. Most people never run the baseline because the result might be unwelcome; the ones who do stop being impressed by averages.

make.tool: A Baseline You'd Be Embarrassed To Submit
make.does: One Python function that takes your model's predictions and the true labels, computes three stupid baselines — constant mean, most frequent label, first row — and prints a per-category table showing which ones your model actually beats and by how much.
make.why: Everything on today's radar comes back to the same missing instrument. KhatianDoc only discovered that five categories had zero capability because someone thought to include a constant-mean control. You will never find your own version of that by reading averages.
make.try: Start with three lines: baseline_majority(y_train), baseline_mean(y_train), and your model's y_pred. Score all three. Then split by category instead of scoring overall — that is the step that actually finds anything. Run it on whichever dataset is nearest to hand, including one you built yourself.
